messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Mercer had spent most of his adult life helping other people make sense of crises, so the assault he experienced at 53 left him especially shaken by how quickly his own confidence in judgment disappeared. He was a social worker in a busy county office in a North American city, married, usually the person colleagues turned to when a situation felt confusing or unsafe. One evening, after leaving a late meeting, he was sexually assaulted in a place he had assumed was routine and ordinary rather than dangerous; the details still came back in fragments, and what he could not get out of his head was not only what was done to him but the humiliating sense of being overpowered and trapped. When he tries to remember it now, he feels the same surge of terror he felt then, and alongside that terror comes an intense shame that makes the memory hard to speak aloud. Daniel says he knows what happened, but when he tries to tell it, the words do not come; he finds himself stopping short, circling around it, and going quiet.

In the weeks afterward, those memories began to shape his days. The more vividly the assault returned, the more he found himself trying to push it out of his mind, only to end up thinking about it even more. He started spending long stretches in rumination about how he might get even with the man who hurt him, not because he had a clear plan, but because the fantasy gave him a brief feeling of having some control over what had been taken from him. At the same time, he became wary of enclosed spaces, especially the small interview rooms and windowless storage areas in his office, where he could feel his chest tighten and his body brace as though he were back in that trapped, helpless state. Daniel began choosing stairs over elevators and avoiding unfamiliar places altogether, telling himself he could not assess the danger there, that it was safer to stay where he knew every exit. Even delays felt loaded with threat; if a client arrived late or his wife was held up on the way home, he immediately assumed something bad was happening.

That sense of danger did not stay abstract. Once he had begun moving through the world as if something terrible might be just behind him, he noticed himself frequently looking over his shoulder, checking behind him in parking lots and on the street, scanning for anyone who might be following. A short walk from his office to the train, which he once made without thought, became a tense ritual of looking back at every crossing and every storefront reflection. The more he monitored for danger, the more real danger seemed to feel, and the more the memory of the assault returned with its old terror and shame attached. Those returns were not calm recollections; they came as flashes that made him feel exposed and contaminated, and each one renewed his urge to shut the whole thing down by force. He pushed the images away, rehearsed revenge in his head, and avoided places where he might feel cornered, yet these efforts only left him more keyed up, more alert for threat, and quicker to interpret ordinary interruptions as signs that something bad was unfolding.

Over time, the cycle reached into work and home. Daniel began declining site visits to unfamiliar neighborhoods, which made him less available to clients and more isolated from colleagues who knew him as steady and dependable. He took longer routes to meetings, checked hallways before entering, and sometimes sat with his back to a wall in the staff lounge. At home, his wife noticed him going quiet when she asked how he was doing, and he would change the subject rather than try to find words for the assault. What had once been a life organized around helping others now felt organized around staying ahead of danger, and the vigilance itself kept the event alive for him: every delay, every closed door, every glance over his shoulder seemed to confirm that the world could turn threatening without warning. That, in turn, made the terror on recall stronger and the shame more crushing, which sent him back to suppression, avoidance, and the private revenge fantasies that briefly soothed him but never settled him.

Daniel finally sought help after a recent evening when he left the office late, found the elevator out of service, and had to decide whether to walk down several dim flights enclosed by concrete walls. He froze on the landing, suddenly convinced someone was behind him, then spent the drive home checking mirrors and imagining what he would do if the assailant ever reappeared. He came to treatment because he is tired of living as though he is still being hunted, and because the shame of not being able to speak about what happened has begun to feel as painful as the memory itself. What he most hopes is that he can recover a sense of safety without having to keep looking over his shoulder all the time.
